bib.title: TURA: Tool-Augmented Unified Retrieval Agent for AI Search

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "TURA: Tool-Augmented Unified Retrieval Agent for AI Search", Zhejun Zhao (first author, equal contribution with Yuchen Li, Alley Liu) et al., Baidu Inc. arXiv:2508.04604v2 (12 Mar 2026). Venue: no venue stated. The header reads "Conference'17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA", which is the ACM template placeholder, so treat it as preprint.

COVERAGE: 10 of 10 pages read, 62,019 of 62,019 chars. References and the appendix prompt templates (A.1 to A.4) were skimmed. The extraction is clean. The only fault is the Figure 1 and Figure 2 text, which came out as jumbled screenshot text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Query-to-server routing (MCP server selection) works because the server index is augmented with synthetic queries, and queries are decomposed first. The full method gets Recall@5 0.8289 and Precision@5 0.9190, against 0.4187 and 0.5505 for plain dense retrieval.
  number: Recall@5 0.4187 -> 0.8289
  setup: MCP-Bench, 61 servers, ERNIE dense retriever, Qwen3-1.7B decomposer; offline.
  quote: "Dense Retrieval (ERNIE) 0.4187 0.5505 / TURA (w/o Augment.) 0.7500 0.8555 / TURA (w/o Decomp.) 0.4530 0.5631 / TURA (Full) 0.8289 0.9190"
  where: p7, Table 4
- Without decomposition, a single vector cannot handle a multi-intent query. The ablation shows decomposition adds about 0.38 recall, and augmentation adds about 0.08 on top of that.
  number: 0.4530 without decomposition vs 0.8289 full
  setup: same as Table 4.
  quote: "Removing decomposition (w/o Decomp.) severely impairs performance, confirming that a single vector cannot handle multi-intent queries."
  where: p7
- Index design for the routing step: about 20 synthetic queries per server is best (the curve plateaus after that). Multi-vector with MaxSim beats single-vector.
  number: Single-Vector 0.7721 vs Multi-Vector (Queries + Doc) 0.8289 Recall@5; N_Q = 20
  quote: "performance peaks at 𝑁𝑄 = 20and then plateaus." and "Single-Vector 0.7721 0.8956 / Multi-Vector (Queries + Doc) 0.8289 0.9190 / Multi-Vector (Queries Only) 0.8299 0.9208"
  setup: synthetic queries generated at temperature above 1.0. The authors keep the server description as a "safety net" even though queries-only scores marginally higher.
  where: p7, Fig 3 and Table 5; method in 4.2.2 to 4.2.4 (p3 to p4)
- A DAG planner cuts latency 44.2% on complex multi-hop queries with no loss in success rate. This subset is small by design: only 4.98% of queries are multi-intent.
  number: 1,650 ms -> 920 ms; success 88.9% -> 89.1%
  setup: complex multi-hop subset of MCP-Bench; planner is Deepseek-V3.
  quote: "Sequential Plan 88.9% 1,650 / DAG Plan 89.1% 920" and "the DAG-based planner reduces average latency by44.2%on these complex queries"
  where: p7 Table 6; p8 text
- A router model decides query complexity. Simple queries skip the DAG planner and get a single-task plan.
  number: none
  quote: "A router model then determines the query's complexity. For queries classified as simple, asingle-task execution plan is constructed without using the DAG planner."
  where: p4, section 4.3
- End-to-end offline, TURA beats LLM+RAG by 22.2 points on human-judged accuracy and 23.8 on faithfulness.
  number: accuracy 87.5% vs 65.3%; faithfulness 96.2% vs 72.4% (human)
  setup: MCP-Bench, 10,683 queries, 61 servers. Baselines are Deepseek-V3 + a Baidu Search API retriever, "Dynamic RAG", and Tool-Agent with the same MCP servers. Judging is human plus LLM on a 3-point scale. Tool-Agent gets 76.8% accuracy and 81.7% faithfulness (human).
  quote: "LLM + RAG 65.3% 68.1% 72.4% 75.0% ... Tool-Agent 76.8% 80.4% 81.7% 83.9% / TURA 87.5% 88.3% 96.2% 97.1%"
  where: p6, Table 1
- Distilled small executor: Qwen3-4B Distilled has 88.3% tool-calling accuracy at 750 ms P80 per step. The teacher (Deepseek-V3) gets 82.4% at 8,700 ms, and GPT-4o gets 81.7% at 6,800 ms. The train-with-thought, infer-without-thought method means rationales are used in SFT, but inference emits the action only.
  number: 70.1% -> 88.3%, 2,200 -> 750 ms (-66%)
  setup: teacher trajectories from Deepseek-V3 filtered by a correctness judge and an efficiency judge. Latency was measured on two NVIDIA L20 GPUs for Qwen, and on the Baidu Qianfan online service for Deepseek-V3. P80 latency.
  quote: "Qwen3-4B Distilled 4B 88.3 750" and "boosts accuracy by +18.2 absolute percentage points over its base counterpart (from 70.1% to 88.3%) while concurrently achieving a 66% reduction in P80 latency (from 2,200ms to 750ms)"
  where: p8, Table 7
- Online A/B test against production LLM+RAG: Session Success Rate 55.1% -> 64.0% (+8.9). GSB is 13% good, 86% same, 4% bad. Total issues fell from 66 to 55 (-16.7%). Critical failures fell from 9 to 4. The largest gains are on travel.
  number: SSR +8.9 points
  setup: only 103 queries sampled, three annotators per query with majority vote. The paper says "statistically significant" but reports no test or interval. The baseline errors cited are weather temperature deviations and train schedule discrepancies.
  quote: "TURA (Ours) 64.0% (+8.9%) 13% / 86% / 4%" and "We sampled 103 queries to balance coverage and cost"
  where: p6 to p7, Tables 2 and 3
- Benchmark shape: most production queries are simple.
  number: 95.02% single-intent, 4.98% multi-intent; average 1.533 tool calls per query (P50=1, P90=3); average DAG width 1.147
  quote: "Queries:10,683total queries, with95.02%single-intent and4.98%multi-intent queries."
  setup: MCP-Bench built from anonymised Baidu logs, Cohen's kappa 0.87, released at github.com/weixiaolong94-hub/TURA.
  where: p5 to p6
- Framing: static web retrieval is itself modelled as one MCP server, so RAG and tools share one planning pipeline. The objective is to maximise answer quality subject to a latency cap.
  number: none
  quote: "traditional web retrieval is itself treated as an MCP server (i.e., a search server)"
  where: p3, Section 3, Eq. 1
- Deployed since May 2025, "serving tens of millions of users". This is the paper's own claim.
  quote: "since May 2025, TURA has been fully deployed, successfully serving tens of millions of users"
  where: p2

LIMITS
- The online A/B test uses 103 queries and gives no significance test, despite the claim of statistical significance.
- Table 1 baselines are the authors' own configurations. The Tool-Agent baseline has no MCP retrieval, so the comparison is partly an ablation of the retrieval module.
- The DAG gain (44.2%) applies only to the rare multi-hop subset. At average DAG width 1.147, most traffic is not helped.
- The 3-point accuracy and faithfulness judgments mix humans and LLM judges.
- No end-to-end latency is reported for the full system, and no cost figures.
- The text says "Table 1 shows the latency impact of the DAG planner", but Table 1 has no latency column. This is an internal inconsistency.
- The student beating the teacher (88.3% vs 82.4%) is attributed to trajectory curation. That was not isolated in an ablation.
- The router's accuracy for simple versus complex queries is not reported.
- Data is Baidu-specific: Chinese-language travel, finance, weather and food APIs, with server identifiers anonymised.
- The authors concede nothing explicitly; there is no limitations section.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al., 2023, ICLR); LLMCompiler (Kim et al., 2024, ICML; the paper cites a 3.6x speedup); ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023); Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023); ADaPT (Prasad et al., 2023); Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024); DRAGIN (Su et al., 2024, ACL); Re-Invoke tool retrieval (Chen et al., 2024); agent distillation (Kang et al., 2025); MAGNET (Yin et al., 2025); least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2022); the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024); Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025); Deepseek-V3 (Liu et al., 2024).

CODE: none in the paper. Appendix A.1 to A.4 hold prompt templates. A.2 is the decomposition prompt, with JSON output {"tasks": [...]}.

FIGURES (the captions script was not run; captions are from the extracted text)
- Fig 1 (p1): "Demonstration of TURA's agentic capabilities". The same train-ticket query is answered through the Ctrip MCP tool and through traditional RAG. This is the quickest picture of why static RAG fails on live data.
- Fig 2 (p4): "TURA Framework Overview". Intent decomposition, then ANN recall over the MCP server store, then a router, then either a simple path or the DAG planner, then a Qwen-4B executor. The worked example is a Beijing trip, where weather runs in parallel and the path planner depends on the attractions and the hotel.
- Fig 3 (p7): recall and precision against the number of synthetic queries per server, peaking at 20.

NOTE TO NOTE 08 (grep of /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/notes/08-agentic-rag-prince.md)
- The strongest point bears on the "Routing" section (line 493, where line 542 says a route description is a document in a very small index, and a wrong route is recall zero). TURA gives the measured version of that claim. Server descriptions are augmented with about 20 synthetic queries, and queries are decomposed first. Recall@5 goes from 0.4187 to 0.8289, and the ablation shows both parts matter. This is also direct evidence for "From one researcher to domain sub-agents" (line 546), where tool lists grow and overlap and selection accuracy falls. TURA's answer is retrieval over tools before the planner sees them, instead of Think & Plan or domain agents.
- The note does not already say it. Grep for DAG, distill, MCP, decompos, index augment, synthetic quer and tool retriev found nothing relevant. The only parallelism mentioned is the 5 parallel hybrid searches at line 132, which is unrelated. TURA is not cited anywhere in the 02-rag-retrieval folder (the grep for "tura" returned no match).
- Secondary: "When agentic RAG pays" (line 690) lists latency as a reason to avoid agentic RAG. TURA is a counterpoint: a DAG plan cuts latency 44.2% (1,650 to 920 ms), and a 4B distilled executor runs at 750 ms per step against 8,700 ms for the teacher. The latency caveat can be softened to "unless parallelised and distilled", with the scope limit that only about 5% of the benchmark is multi-intent.
- Related note: the router type table (lines 499 to 505) lists a semantic router (cosine against route descriptions). TURA is a semantic router with augmented routes (MaxSim over multi-vector embeddings) plus an LLM decomposer.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions were found. Figures 1 and 2 extracted as jumbled screenshot text, so I reconstructed their structure from the Figure 2 caption only.
